specPoints.text: understand, in terms of intermolecular forces, physical properties shown by substances, including: i the trends in boiling temperatures of alkanes with increasing chain length ii the effect of branching in the carbon chain on the boiling temperatures of alkanes iii the relatively low volatility (higher boiling temperatures) of alcohols compared to alkanes with a similar number of electrons iv the trends in boiling temperatures of the hydrogen halides HF to HI

primer.text: Boiling point is a tally of intermolecular strength, so three levers move it: how much surface a molecule exposes, how many electrons it carries, and whether it can hydrogen bond. This note applies each lever to alkanes, alcohols and the hydrogen halides, and shows why HF breaks the trend line its own group follows.

lessons.title: Chain shape and electron count
lessons.opening: Two levers control the London contribution to boiling point: how much of the molecule touches its neighbours, and how many electrons it drags around. This lesson works both, comparing branched against straight chains and reading the noble-gas and alkane graphs.
keyPoints: Larger molecular surface area means more contact with adjacent molecules and stronger induced attractions.
Branching reduces surface area, weakening London forces and lowering boiling points.
More electrons raise the chance and size of temporary dipoles, strengthening induced forces.
Boiling points of the noble gases climb as electron counts grow.
The alkane graph shows the same climb: longer chains boil higher.

low.restatement: A stretched chain touches many neighbours and its many electrons flicker strongly, so it boils high; a branched or small-electron molecule touches less and boils lower.
low.analogy: A long plank lying flat touches the whole shelf beneath it, while a crumpled ball of the same wood touches only at a few points - plank chains stick, ball chains roll apart.
low.examPointer: For isomer comparisons, hold the electron count equal and argue only through surface area - mixing the two levers loses the comparison mark.

medium.restatement: Contact area scales the induced-dipole interaction, so branching lowers it at fixed formula; electron count sets both the frequency and magnitude of instantaneous dipoles, which is why the noble-gas series climbs monotonically.
medium.analogy: A wide paintbrush covers a wall in one stroke (large contact, strong grip) while a slim brush needs many passes; heavier pigment (more electrons) makes every stroke grip harder.
medium.examPointer: Quote both graphs' message in one line: boiling point rises with electron count and falls with branching - then name the force responsible, London dispersion.

check.stem: How does branching affect a molecule's boiling point?

options.text: It lowers the boiling point by shrinking surface area
options.explanation: Fewer contact points weaken the induced attractions between branched molecules.

options.text: It raises the boiling point by adding bonds
options.explanation: Bond count inside the molecule does not set the boiling point.

options.text: It leaves the boiling point unchanged
options.explanation: Isomers with different shapes boil at different temperatures.

options.text: It removes electrons from the molecule
options.explanation: Branching rearranges the same atoms, keeping the electron count.

check.stem: Why do heavier noble gases boil higher than lighter ones?

options.text: More electrons give stronger and more frequent temporary dipoles
options.explanation: Growing electron clouds raise the induced attraction down the group.

options.text: Their nuclei carry positive charge that attracts neighbours
options.explanation: Nuclear charge stays internal; the interatomic pull is induced-dipole based.

options.text: They hydrogen bond in the liquid
options.explanation: Noble gases carry no hydrogen at all.
Thermal expansion is a consequence, not a cause.

check.stem: What is the relationship between molecular surface area and induced dipole strength?

options.text: Larger area means more contact and stronger induced forces
options.explanation: Contact area is the multiplier on the London interaction.
More contact strengthens, not weakens, the attraction.

options.text: Area has no bearing on the forces
options.explanation: The contact-points diagram exists precisely because it does.
Rearranging the same atoms preserves the count.

check.stem: Two isomers share a formula and electron count but boil 25 degrees apart. What explains the gap?

options.text: The straighter isomer contacts neighbours over more area
options.explanation: At equal electrons, surface area decides the induced contribution.

options.text: The straighter isomer has more electrons
options.explanation: Identical formulas fix identical electron counts.
No O-H, N-H or H-F group appears in either.
Systematic isomer gaps are real chemistry.

check.stem: Which pair of changes both raise a hydrocarbon's boiling point?

options.explanation: Both grow surface contact and electron count effects.
Branching cancels the chain-length gain by shrinking contact.
The shorter chain cuts electron count and lowers the point.
Both changes push the boiling point down.

check.stem: State the effect of branching on boiling temperature and name the force involved.
check.modelAnswer: Branching lowers the boiling temperature because it reduces the surface area over which London dispersion forces can act.

check.stem: State what happens to temporary dipoles as electron count increases.
check.modelAnswer: A greater electron count makes distortions more likely and bigger, so temporary dipoles are larger and more frequent and the induced forces strengthen.

check.stem: Explain why the alkane boiling-point graph climbs with chain length.
check.modelAnswer: Each extra carbon brings more electrons and more molecular surface, so both the size and the contact area of induced interactions grow, and the boiling point rises with every added CH2 unit.

check.stem: Pentane boils at 36 degrees while its branched isomer 2-methylbutane boils at 28 degrees. How much branching credit, in degrees, does the straight chain claim in this pair?
check.modelAnswer: The 8-degree gap is the branching premium: the straight chain's larger contact area holds it liquid to a higher temperature.

lessons.title: Why alcohols outboil their alkanes
lessons.opening: Swap one CH2 for an OH and the boiling point leaps tens of degrees. This lesson traces the jump to hydrogen bonding between alcohol molecules, against the mere induced pulls their alkane cousins manage.
keyPoints: Alcohols carry O-H bonds, so their molecules hydrogen bond to each other.
The oxygen pulls the shared electrons away, leaving each hydrogen delta-positive.
Those hydrogens reach lone pairs on neighbouring oxygens, forming hydrogen bonds.
Alkanes manage only induced dipole-dipole forces between their molecules.
Propane boils at -42 degrees while propanol reaches 97 degrees.

low.restatement: The O-H group lets alcohol molecules hook together strongly; alkane molecules only nudge each other, so separating alcohols takes far more energy.
low.analogy: Alcohol molecules shake hands firmly across the gap; alkane molecules brush sleeves. Undoing handshakes costs more effort than brushing sleeves apart.
low.examPointer: Name both the force in the alcohol (hydrogen bonding) and the force in the alkane (induced dipole-dipole) - naming only one loses the comparison mark.

medium.restatement: Electronegative oxygen polarises the O-H bond, giving hydrogen enough positive character to bond a lone pair on the next molecule's oxygen; the alkane's C-H bonds stay essentially non-polar, so induced forces remain its only intermolecular resource.
medium.analogy: One molecule carries a key ring (delta-positive hydrogens) and the next carries the locks (lone pairs); the alkane has neither keys nor locks and relies on leaning against its neighbour.
medium.examPointer: Quote the propane/propanol figures when asked for evidence - the 139-degree spread is the numbers behind the mechanism.

check.stem: Which intermolecular force dominates between alcohol molecules?

options.text: Hydrogen bonding through the O-H groups
options.explanation: Polarised hydrogens reach lone pairs on neighbouring oxygens.
That is the alkane's ceiling, not the alcohol's.
Alcohols are covalent molecular liquids.
No metal atoms participate.

check.stem: Why is the hydrogen of an O-H group delta-positive?

options.text: Oxygen draws the shared electron pair toward itself
options.explanation: High electronegativity leaves hydrogen's positive end exposed.
The pair is shared, not surrendered.
Repulsion is not the polarity mechanism.
Carbon is not part of the O-H bond.

check.stem: Propane boils at -42 degrees and propanol at 97 degrees. What is the dominant reason for the 139-degree gap?

options.text: Propanol's molecules hydrogen bond while propane's only induce dipoles
options.explanation: The force upgrade is the whole story.
The electron difference is minor; the force type does the heavy lifting.
Covalent strength does not set boiling points.
It is a covalent molecule.

check.stem: Which statement about alkane intermolecular forces is correct?

options.text: Their only intermolecular forces are induced dipole-dipole
options.explanation: No permanent dipoles or O-H groups exist in a pure alkane.
C-H bonds are never hydrogen-bond donors.
The hydrocarbon skeleton is non-polar.

options.text: Their molecules attract by ion-induced dipole
options.explanation: No ions are present.

check.stem: What structural feature must a molecule carry to hydrogen bond?

options.text: Hydrogen attached to O, N or F
options.explanation: That kit is the donor requirement.
C-H hydrogens never qualify.
Unsaturation plays no role in hydrogen bonding.
Neutral alcohols hydrogen bond readily.

check.stem: Name the force that sets alcohol boiling points above alkane boiling points.
check.modelAnswer: Hydrogen bonding between alcohol molecules sets their boiling points far above the induced dipole-dipole ceiling of alkanes.

check.stem: Quote the boiling points of propane and propanol.
check.modelAnswer: Propane boils at -42 degrees and propanol at 97 degrees, a 139-degree demonstration of the hydrogen-bond premium.

check.stem: Explain why replacing a hydrogen of an alkane by an OH group changes the intermolecular force inventory.
check.modelAnswer: The OH group adds a polar O-H bond whose hydrogen reaches oxygen lone pairs on neighbours, so hydrogen bonding joins the inventory; the pure alkane carried only induced dipole-dipole forces.

check.stem: If ethanol boils at 78 degrees and its same-electron-count alkane analogue boils at -24 degrees, how many degrees of hydrogen-bond premium does ethanol show?
check.modelAnswer: Subtracting -24 from 78 gives 102 degrees, the hydrogen-bond premium this comparison displays.

lessons.title: The hydrogen halides and their outlier
lessons.opening: From HCl to HI the boiling points climb smoothly as electrons accumulate - but HF breaks the pattern, boiling hundreds of degrees above its slot. This lesson assigns each force its share of the credit.
keyPoints: The hydrogen halides' boiling points rise from HCl through HBr to HI.
Larger halogens carry more electrons, so induced dipole-dipole forces strengthen along the series.
HF sits far above the trend because its molecules hydrogen bond.
The H-F bond is highly polar, leaving hydrogen strongly positive.
Fluorine's small, intense lone pairs complete the hydrogen-bond link between neighbours.

low.restatement: Down the halogen group the molecules fatten with electrons, so induced forces and boiling points rise together; HF jumps off the line because only it can hydrogen bond.
low.analogy: Three siblings grow steadily heavier with age (HCl, HBr, HI), but the youngest (HF) carries a backpack no sibling has - the hydrogen-bond kit - and outweighs them all.
low.examPointer: Sketch the graph with HF plotted as a high outlier above the HCl-HI line, then label the outlier 'hydrogen bonding'.

medium.restatement: Electron count drives the induced contribution from chlorine to iodine; in HF the bond polarity concentrates charge at hydrogen and fluorine's compact lone pairs accept a link, adding an entirely new force channel that dominates the boiling point.
medium.analogy: The series adds passengers one by one (electrons), but HF also bolted on a tow bar (hydrogen bonding) that hauls its boiling point clear of the queue.
medium.examPointer: Say 'hydrogen bonds between HF molecules' explicitly - 'polarity alone' explanations fail because HCl is also polar yet sits on the trend line.

check.stem: Which hydrogen halide boils highest?

options.explanation: Hydrogen bonding lifts HF far above every neighbour on the series.
HCl sits at the trend line's low end.
HBr is an intermediate on the line.
HI tops the induced-only trend but not HF.

check.stem: Why do the boiling points of HCl, HBr and HI increase in order?

options.text: Each molecule carries more electrons, strengthening induced forces
options.explanation: Electron count climbs down the group and so does the dispersion pull.
None of the three hydrogen bonds at all.
Bonds lengthen down the group.
Polarity actually falls as the halogen gets bigger.

check.stem: What two features of fluorine make strong hydrogen bonds possible in HF?

options.text: High bond polarity and small intense lone pairs
options.explanation: The polar bond exposes hydrogen; the compact lone pairs accept the link.
Fluorine is small and strongly electronegative.

options.text: Low electron count and high mass
options.explanation: Mass is irrelevant; the count is nine.
Fluorine has neither.

check.stem: HCl is a polar molecule yet sits on the trend line. Why does polarity alone not lift it?

options.text: Its polarity supports only permanent dipole-dipole forces, which beat induced ones modestly at equal size
options.explanation: Without hydrogen bonding there is no premium.

options.text: HCl's polarity is too weak to matter at all
options.explanation: The polarity does contribute; it just cannot add the hydrogen-bond premium.

options.text: HCl carries hydrogen bonds like HF
options.explanation: Chlorine's diffuse lone pairs cannot form them.
Permanent dipoles do raise points above the induced baseline.

check.stem: Which statement about the hydrogen halide graph is correct?

options.text: HCl, HBr and HI rise steadily while HF plots far above the extrapolated line
options.explanation: The smooth climb plus the outlier is exactly the data shape.

options.text: All four sit on one straight line
options.explanation: HF's outlier breaks the line.
HF boils highest of all four.
HI boils highest of the induced-only trio.

check.stem: State the force responsible for the smooth HCl-to-HI climb and the force responsible for HF's outlier position.
check.modelAnswer: Induced dipole-dipole forces drive the smooth climb, and hydrogen bonding accounts for HF's outlier position.

check.stem: Describe what the fluorine end of an HF molecule offers to a neighbour.
check.modelAnswer: Fluorine offers small, intense lone pairs that accept the hydrogen bond from a neighbouring molecule's polarised hydrogen.

check.stem: Explain why HF's boiling point exceeds HI's despite HI's far greater electron count.
check.modelAnswer: HI's electron advantage strengthens only induced forces, whereas HF gains a whole extra force channel - hydrogen bonding - whose energy outweighs the electron-count deficit and hoists HF above the whole series.

check.stem: If HF's hydrogen-bond premium adds roughly 180 degrees above its trend-line slot of about -80 degrees, estimate HF's actual boiling point.
check.modelAnswer: Adding the premium to the slot gives about 100 degrees, close to HF's observed boiling point near 20 degrees once the trend slope is folded in.

glossary.definition: The induced dipole-dipole attraction whose strength scales with electron count and molecular contact area.
A skeletal rearrangement that shrinks molecular surface area and so weakens induced attractions between isomers.
The boiling-point excess a substance shows above its trend line because its molecules hydrogen bond.
